# kernmini_magics


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Run a kernmini shell inside IPython as a `%%magic`: the same engine as
the standalone kernel, from a Python notebook.

## Developer Guide

If you are new to using `nbdev` here are some useful pointers to get you
started.

### Install kernmini_magics in Development mode

``` sh
# make sure kernmini_magics package is installed in development mode
$ pip install -e .

# make changes under nbs/ directory
# ...

# compile to have changes apply to kernmini_magics
$ nbdev_prepare
```

## Usage

### Installation

Install latest from the GitHub
[repository](https://github.com/Rahuketu86/kernmini_magics):

``` sh
$ pip install git+https://github.com/Rahuketu86/kernmini_magics.git
```

or from [conda](https://anaconda.org/Rahuketu86/kernmini_magics)

``` sh
$ conda install -c Rahuketu86 kernmini_magics
```

or from [pypi](https://pypi.org/project/kernmini_magics/)

``` sh
$ pip install kernmini_magics
```

### Documentation

Documentation can be found hosted on this GitHub
[repository](https://github.com/Rahuketu86/kernmini_magics)’s
[pages](https://Rahuketu86.github.io/kernmini_magics/). Additionally you
can find package manager specific guidelines on
[conda](https://anaconda.org/Rahuketu86/kernmini_magics) and
[pypi](https://pypi.org/project/kernmini_magics/) respectively.

## How to use

A [kernmini](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/kernmini) shell – the object
with `execute()` / `complete()` / `inspect()` / `set_stream_sender()` /
`interrupt()` that kernmini serves as a Jupyter kernel – can also run
inside an ordinary IPython kernel.
[`Workspace`](https://Rahuketu86.github.io/kernmini_magics/core.html#workspace)
wraps one as a `%name` / `%%name` magic plus a Python object, so a
Python notebook can mix in another language and call back and forth.
Each kernmini kernel repo defines its own magic on top of this:

Each is loaded explicitly, e.g. `%load_ext prolog_wasm_kernmini.magics`,
and installed with that package’s `magics` extra. Each repo’s
`nbs/11_demo_python_magic.ipynb` is a Python dialog using its magic.

### What every magic does

- **`%%name` cell / `%name` line.** The cell runs in the kernel’s own
  shell, so state persists across cells exactly as in the standalone
  kernel. The line form, and calling the object (`prolog("...")`),
  return a string: the implicit result’s text, or for Prolog the answer
  text.
- **Errors** raise a per-language
  [`MagicError`](https://Rahuketu86.github.io/kernmini_magics/core.html#magicerror)
  subclass (`PrologError`, `SchemeError`, `JSError`, `MicroPythonError`,
  `ClangError`) after any output produced before the error; `e.output`
  holds that output. IPython shows the kernel’s message, not Python
  frames.
- **A trailing quiet marker** hides the implicit result, as in basedpl’s
  and IPython’s own magics; output the code prints itself still shows.
- **`obj.register(fn)`** (also a decorator) makes a Python function
  callable from the other language. It does in a Python kernel what a
  `%%host` cell does in the standalone kernel; `%%host` itself is
  unchanged there.
- **Ctrl-C** stops a runaway cell through the shell’s `interrupt()`.
  **`obj.timeout`** (seconds, off by default; env `<NAME>_MAGIC_TIMEOUT`
  or `KERNMINI_MAGIC_TIMEOUT`) does the same on a deadline and raises
  `TimeoutError`. The workspace stays usable after both.
- **Completion** inside a magic cell uses the shell’s `complete()`;
  `obj.names(prefix)` returns the same names.
- **`%name --reset`** / `obj.reset()` starts a fresh shell.

### Defining a magic for a kernel

``` python
from kernmini_magics import Workspace, MagicError

class FooError(MagicError): "A failed Foo cell."

def _make_shell():
    from .core import FooKernminiShell      # the kernel's own shell class, unchanged
    return FooKernminiShell()

async def _register(shell, name, fn):         # optional: expose a Python callable to Foo
    await shell._ensure_context()
    shell._rt.register(name, fn)

foo = Workspace('foo', _make_shell, error_cls=FooError, register=_register,
                quiet_marker=';', strip_marker=True)

def load_ipython_extension(ip): foo.load(ip)
```

[`Workspace`](https://Rahuketu86.github.io/kernmini_magics/core.html#workspace)
arguments:

- `quiet_marker` / `strip_marker` – the trailing marker that hides the
  result (`None` for none), and whether to remove it before running (for
  languages where it would be meaningless or invalid).
- `call_returns` – `'result'` (default: return the implicit result’s
  text, print output) or `'output'` (return the printed text itself, not
  echoed).
- `aliases` – more magic names for the same engine.
- `timeout` – default deadline in seconds; otherwise read from the
  environment.

A shell that accepts `quiet=` in `execute()` is told when the marker was
used, so it can hide results it prints as output (Prolog’s bindings). A
shell with `interrupt()` gets real Ctrl-C; without it, the running task
is cancelled.

### How it works

- Every shell call runs on one private daemon thread with its own event
  loop, so a synchronous magic can drive async shells without
  `asyncio.run()` inside ipykernel’s running loop, and a thread-bound
  engine always sees the same thread.
- Output events cross to the main thread through a queue and are printed
  there, so they are attributed to the running cell.
- While a magic waits, it installs `signal.default_int_handler` for
  SIGINT: for magic cells ipykernel installs a handler that cancels the
  cell’s asyncio future, which never takes effect while a blocking magic
  holds the thread.
- The completion matcher works out the text before the cursor from
  IPython’s line + column coordinates and filters the shell’s reply to
  the typed fragment (names starting with it, else names containing it),
  since some shells rely on the frontend to filter.
